Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Iraq's government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit to Washington amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, an Iraqi government spokesman said Tuesday. Students protest the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad's Mustansiriya University. Ali al-Dabbagh said the Iraqi government approved several amendments that were "necessary, essential and appropriate" to the draft status-of-forces agreement, which would set the terms for U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate on their presence expires at the end of this year. "The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests," al-Dabbagh said. It is unclear when al-Maliki will submit the changes to the draft document. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said that there was "great reluctance" to make any more changes to the agreement. However, senior U.S. officials -- speaking under the condition of anonymity -- are not ruling out possibly renegotiating parts of the deal with Iraq if the country's parliament does not approve it. The most vocal opponent of the draft security deal in Iraq has been the political party of radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which opposes any U.S. military presence in Iraq. U.S. military helicopters Tuesday flew over Baghdad's Mustansiriya University, where hundreds of students took part in a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement against the status-of-forces deal. "We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty," said law student Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, one of the demonstrators. Fellow demonstrator and law student Hisham Mohammed said the students plan to organize a sit-in and a strike across universities in Iraq to protest the agreement. The draft status-of-forces agreement, according to a copy obtained by CNN, calls for U.S. combat troops to be out of Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and out of the country entirely by December 31, 2011. The agreement allows for an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces' stay in Iraq, by agreement of both parties. It also allows the Iraqi government to ask "the United States government to leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces." Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces in Iraq has been a sticking point in the negotiation, with the U.S. side preferring that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. Baghdad had sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit major crimes in the course of their duties. Under the draft agreement, U.S. forces or contractors who commit "major and premeditated murders" while off duty and outside U.S. facilities would fall under Iraqi jurisdiction, according to the copy obtained by CNN. All other crimes -- and murders committed inside U.S. facilities or by on-duty forces -- would fall under American jurisdiction, the agreement says.

**BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN)** — Iraq’s government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to present Washington with amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, an Iraqi government spokesman said Tuesday.

Students protested the status-of-forces agreement Tuesday at Baghdad’s Mustansiriya University.

Ali al-Dabbagh said the Iraqi government had approved several amendments it deemed “necessary, essential and appropriate” to the draft status-of-forces agreement, which would establish the terms governing U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate for their presence expires at the end of this year.

“The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests,” al-Dabbagh said.

It remains unclear when al-Maliki will submit the proposed changes to the draft document.

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates recently said there was “great reluctance” to make any further changes to the agreement. However, senior U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, have not ruled out the possibility of renegotiating parts of the deal with Iraq if the country’s parliament does not approve it.

The most outspoken opponent of the draft security agreement in Iraq has been the political party of radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which opposes any U.S. military presence in Iraq.

On Tuesday, U.S. military helicopters flew over Baghdad’s Mustansiriya University, where hundreds of students participated in a demonstration organized by the Sadr movement against the status-of-forces agreement.

“We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty,” said law student Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, one of the demonstrators.

Another demonstrator, law student Hisham Mohammed, said the students planned to organize a sit-in and a strike across universities in Iraq to protest the agreement.

The draft status-of-forces agreement, according to a copy obtained by CNN, calls for U.S. combat troops to withdraw from Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and to leave the country entirely by December 31, 2011.

The agreement allows for either an earlier withdrawal or an extension of the U.S. forces’ presence in Iraq, subject to the consent of both parties. It also permits the Iraqi government to ask “the United States government to leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces.”

Legal jurisdiction over U.S. forces in Iraq has been a central point of contention in the negotiations, with the U.S. side preferring that its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law.

Baghdad had sought the authority to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes unrelated to official military operations, as well as jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit major crimes in the course of their duties.

Under the draft agreement, U.S. forces or contractors who commit “major and premeditated murders” while off duty and outside U.S. facilities would fall under Iraqi jurisdiction, according to the copy obtained by CNN.

All other crimes — as well as murders committed inside U.S. facilities or by on-duty forces — would fall under American jurisdiction, the agreement says.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — An Iraqi government representative said Tuesday that Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki has been given permission by Iraq’s government to present proposed revisions to Washington on a draft security pact with the United States.

On Tuesday, students demonstrated at Baghdad’s Mustansiriya University against the proposed status-of-forces agreement.

Government spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh said Iraq’s government had accepted a number of changes to the draft agreement, describing them as “necessary, essential and appropriate.” The agreement is intended to define the role and conditions of U.S. troops in Iraq after the United Nations authorization for their presence ends at the close of this year.

“The Iraqi government authorizes the prime minister to bring up these amendments to the U.S. side in order to reach a draft agreement that will preserve the fundamental principles and the sovereignty of Iraq and its high interests,” al-Dabbagh said.

It is not yet known when al-Maliki will formally deliver the proposed revisions. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has recently said there is “great reluctance” to make further alterations to the deal. Still, senior American officials, speaking anonymously, have not dismissed the possibility of reopening negotiations on parts of the agreement if Iraq’s parliament refuses to approve it.

Inside Iraq, the strongest criticism of the draft security arrangement has come from the political movement loyal to radical Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, which rejects any continued U.S. military presence in the country.

On Tuesday, U.S. military helicopters circled above Mustansiriya University in Baghdad as hundreds of students joined a protest against the status-of-forces deal organized by the Sadr movement.

“We are against this agreement between the Iraqi government and between the American government because it is against Iraqi sovereignty,” said Ahmed Fadhil Abbas, a law student who took part in the protest.

Another law student and demonstrator, Hisham Mohammed, said students intend to stage a sit-in and a strike at universities across Iraq to oppose the agreement.

According to a copy of the draft status-of-forces agreement obtained by CNN, U.S. combat forces would have to withdraw from Iraqi cities and villages by July 30, 2009, and leave Iraq completely by December 31, 2011.

The draft also permits the withdrawal date to be moved earlier or the U.S. troop presence to be extended, provided both sides agree. In addition, it allows Iraq’s government to request that “the United States government leave certain forces for training and for support purposes for the Iraqi forces.”

One major obstacle in the talks has been the question of legal authority over U.S. personnel in Iraq. The United States has favored keeping its troops and contractors exempt from Iraqi law. Baghdad, however, has pushed for the right to detain and prosecute Americans accused of crimes unrelated to official military missions, as well as authority over troops and contractors who commit serious offenses while performing their duties.

Under the draft obtained by CNN, Iraqi courts would have jurisdiction over U.S. forces or contractors who commit “major and premeditated murders” while off duty and outside American facilities.

The agreement states that all other offenses, including killings committed inside U.S. facilities or by personnel on duty, would remain under U.S. legal authority.

Iraq’s government has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to present what it described as “necessary” amendments to a draft security agreement with the United States, a pact intended to define the legal basis for the presence of American troops in Iraq after the expiration of the current United Nations mandate.

The decision reflects Baghdad’s effort to ensure that any final agreement protects Iraqi sovereignty and national interests. The proposed status-of-forces agreement is expected to set the rules for U.S. military operations, the legal status of American personnel, and the broader framework for cooperation between the two countries once the U.N. authorization ends.

Iraqi officials have indicated that the cabinet wants changes to the draft before it can move forward. The amendments are aimed at addressing concerns that the deal could leave too much authority in American hands or fail to give Iraq sufficient control over foreign forces operating on its territory.

The issue has become one of the most sensitive political questions facing the Iraqi government. While the United States has signaled reluctance to reopen negotiations after months of talks, Iraqi leaders face intense pressure at home to demand stronger guarantees. Many Iraqi political factions are wary of any agreement that could be seen as prolonging the U.S. military presence or limiting Iraq’s independence.

Opposition has been especially strong from the movement led by Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, a longtime critic of the U.S. presence in Iraq. Sadr’s supporters have denounced the proposed agreement and have called for the withdrawal of American troops, arguing that any long-term security arrangement with Washington risks undermining Iraqi sovereignty.

The dispute underscores the political fragility of the draft accord. For Maliki, the challenge is to balance Iraq’s continued need for security support with widespread public and parliamentary suspicion of a formal agreement with the United States. For Washington, the agreement is crucial because the U.N. mandate that currently provides legal cover for U.S.-led forces is due to expire, making a new arrangement necessary if American troops are to remain in the country.

The cabinet’s authorization gives Maliki room to seek changes, but it does not guarantee that the United States will accept them or that Iraqi lawmakers will ultimately approve the pact. The outcome will play a major role in shaping the future of the U.S. military presence in Iraq and the broader relationship between Baghdad and Washington.

**Iraq seeks changes to draft U.S. troop agreement amid campus protests**

**BAGHDAD, Iraq** — Iraq’s Cabinet has authorized Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki to submit proposed amendments to a draft security agreement that would govern the presence of U.S. forces in Iraq after the expiration of the U.N. mandate, Iraqi officials said.

The decision came as political pressure mounted in Baghdad over the proposed U.S.-Iraq status-of-forces agreement, which sets a timetable for the withdrawal of American troops and outlines the legal rules under which they would operate.

Under the draft accord, U.S. combat forces would withdraw from Iraqi cities and towns by **June 30, 2009**, and all U.S. troops would leave Iraq by **December 31, 2011**, unless both governments agreed to alter the arrangement.

The agreement also addresses one of the most sensitive issues in the negotiations: legal jurisdiction over U.S. personnel. According to Iraqi officials familiar with the draft, Iraq would have jurisdiction over U.S. troops accused of serious crimes committed while off duty and off base. The United States would retain jurisdiction over troops acting on duty or inside U.S. facilities. U.S. contractors, a major point of Iraqi public anger after several deadly incidents, would be subject to Iraqi law under the draft.

Al-Maliki’s government has not publicly detailed all of the amendments it plans to seek, but Iraqi lawmakers have said the requested changes involve sovereignty, legal authority and assurances that Iraqi territory will not be used to launch attacks against neighboring countries.

The pact has faced opposition from several Iraqi political factions, including followers of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, who have demanded a faster and unconditional U.S. withdrawal.

On the campus of **Mustansiriya University** in eastern Baghdad, students staged protests against the agreement, chanting slogans and carrying banners rejecting what they described as any long-term foreign military presence in Iraq. The demonstration reflected broader unease among many Iraqis who view the accord as a test of the country’s sovereignty more than five years after the U.S.-led invasion.

Supporters of the agreement say it is necessary to prevent a legal vacuum once the U.N. mandate expires at the end of the year and to provide an orderly framework for the withdrawal of U.S. forces. Without a deal or a renewed U.N. mandate, U.S. troops would lack a clear legal basis to remain in Iraq.

The draft agreement must still be approved by Iraq’s parliament, where debate is expected to be heated. U.S. officials have said the negotiated text reflects months of compromise, but Iraqi leaders have indicated they want further revisions before sending it to lawmakers for a final vote.

That mandate is set to expire at the end of the year, increasing pressure on Baghdad and Washington to finalize a new framework before the deadline.

Iraqi government officials said the approved amendments are intended to address concerns raised by political blocs over sovereignty, legal jurisdiction and the timetable for U.S. troop withdrawals. The revised language is expected to be sent to Washington for review before the agreement is presented for final approval by Iraq’s parliament.

The proposed pact, often described as a security agreement or status-of-forces arrangement, would define the rights and responsibilities of U.S. troops operating in Iraq once the U.N. mandate ends. Without a new agreement, the legal authority for American military operations, detentions and movements inside Iraq would be thrown into uncertainty.

Iraqi leaders have insisted that any deal must recognize Iraq’s sovereignty and place clear limits on the activities of foreign forces. Among the most sensitive issues have been whether U.S. troops could conduct operations without Iraqi approval, how detainees would be handled, and whether American personnel could face Iraqi courts under certain circumstances.

The agreement has been the subject of heated debate in Baghdad. Supporters argue it is necessary to ensure stability as Iraqi security forces continue to assume greater responsibility across the country. Opponents, including some nationalist and religious factions, have warned that the pact could prolong the American military presence and undermine Iraqi independence.

Prime Ministerial officials said the latest changes reflect Iraq’s demand for a stronger role in approving military operations and a clearer path toward ending the foreign troop presence. The amendments reportedly include language reinforcing that U.S. forces would not use Iraqi territory to launch attacks on neighboring countries and that combat operations would be coordinated with the Iraqi government.

U.S. officials have said Washington is committed to reaching an agreement that respects Iraqi sovereignty while allowing American forces to continue supporting Iraqi security forces and counterterrorism efforts during the transition.

The pact still faces political hurdles. Iraq’s parliament must approve the final text, and lawmakers are expected to scrutinize the terms closely. Several blocs have demanded guarantees that the agreement will not create permanent U.S. bases in Iraq or allow an indefinite troop presence.

The expiration of the U.N. mandate has made the negotiations urgent. Since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion, foreign military operations in Iraq have been authorized through U.N. Security Council resolutions requested by the Iraqi government. Iraqi leaders have said they do not want to renew that mandate again, preferring instead a bilateral agreement that places the relationship with Washington on a more conventional legal footing.

If finalized, the agreement would represent a major turning point in U.S.-Iraqi relations, shifting the American military presence from an international mandate to terms negotiated directly with the Iraqi state. It would also set the stage for future decisions on troop withdrawals, military cooperation and Iraq’s broader security policy.

For now, the approval of changes by the Iraqi government signals progress — but not a final deal. The next test will come when Washington responds to the amended draft and Iraqi lawmakers decide whether to endorse it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a detailed article about the 2008 U.S.-Iraq security pact negotiations, focusing on Maliki’s authorization to present amendments, U.S. reluctance to renegotiate, withdrawal deadlines, and jurisdiction over American troops.
counterfactuals.output:
# The 2008 U.S.–Iraq Security Pact Negotiations: Amendments, Deadlines, and Jurisdiction

In 2008, the United States and Iraq negotiated one of the most consequential agreements of the post-invasion period: a security pact that would define the legal basis for the presence of American troops in Iraq after the expiration of the United Nations mandate at the end of that year. The negotiations produced what became known as the U.S.–Iraq Status of Forces Agreement, or SOFA, formally titled the **Agreement Between the United States of America and the Republic of Iraq on the Withdrawal of United States Forces from Iraq and the Organization of Their Activities during Their Temporary Presence in Iraq**.

The pact was politically sensitive in both countries, but especially in Iraq, where Prime Minister **Nouri al-Maliki** faced intense pressure from rival political blocs, Shiite religious authorities, Sunni leaders, Kurdish parties, and nationalist factions opposed to any open-ended U.S. military presence. Four issues dominated the late-stage negotiations: Maliki’s authorization to seek amendments, Washington’s reluctance to reopen the text, deadlines for withdrawal, and Iraqi jurisdiction over U.S. troops.

## Background: Why a Security Pact Was Needed

Since the 2003 invasion, U.S.-led coalition forces had operated in Iraq under a series of United Nations Security Council resolutions. These resolutions provided international legal authority for foreign forces to remain in the country. But by 2008, both Washington and Baghdad wanted to move away from the U.N. framework and place the U.S. military presence on a bilateral legal footing.

For Iraq, the transition was tied to sovereignty. Iraqi leaders wanted to show that foreign forces were no longer operating above or outside Iraqi authority. For the United States, the agreement was necessary to protect troops legally and operationally once the U.N. mandate expired on **December 31, 2008**.

Negotiations began months earlier, but they became especially contentious in the autumn of 2008 as Iraqi political factions reviewed the proposed text.

## Maliki’s Authorization to Present Amendments

By October 2008, the draft agreement had been negotiated at the executive level, but Maliki faced growing domestic resistance. Iraqi critics argued that the agreement still gave the United States too much freedom of action and insufficiently recognized Iraqi sovereignty.

Under this pressure, Maliki sought and received political authorization to present amendments to the United States. This authorization came after consultations with Iraq’s major political leaders and governing institutions, including figures in the presidency council, cabinet, and parliamentary blocs.

The decision reflected Maliki’s political balancing act. He did not want to reject the agreement outright, because failure to reach a deal could create a legal vacuum after the U.N. mandate expired. At the same time, he needed to show Iraqi lawmakers and the public that he was not simply accepting American terms.

The amendments Iraq sought focused on several core areas:

1. **Clearer withdrawal timelines for U.S. forces**  
2. **Greater Iraqi authority over military operations**  
3. **Stronger limits on U.S. detention powers**  
4. **Expanded Iraqi legal jurisdiction over American personnel**  
5. **Language emphasizing Iraqi sovereignty and preventing use of Iraqi territory to attack neighboring states**

Maliki’s move to seek amendments was therefore not merely procedural. It was a political necessity, intended to secure enough support in the Iraqi parliament for ratification.

## U.S. Reluctance to Renegotiate

The United States was reluctant to reopen the agreement. American negotiators had already made significant concessions, especially on withdrawal timelines and legal jurisdiction. By late October 2008, U.S. officials described the draft as essentially final and warned that further changes could jeopardize the deal.

Washington’s reluctance had several causes.

First, the Bush administration believed it had already compromised substantially. Earlier U.S. preferences had involved a more flexible, conditions-based military presence. Iraqi insistence on firm dates had pushed the agreement toward a defined withdrawal schedule.

Second, reopening the text risked unraveling a fragile compromise. Any new concession to Iraq could trigger concerns in Washington, especially among military officials who worried about restrictions on troop operations and exposure of U.S. personnel to Iraqi courts.

Third, time was running out. The U.N. mandate was due to expire at the end of 2008. Without a new agreement, the legal authority for U.S. forces to conduct operations, detain suspects, and remain in Iraq would become uncertain.

As a result, U.S. officials initially signaled that the text could not be substantially renegotiated. They indicated that Washington might consider clarifications or interpretive language, but not a wholesale rewriting of the pact.

Still, because Iraqi approval was essential, the United States eventually accepted some modifications and assurances. The final agreement incorporated language that addressed Iraqi concerns without fundamentally changing the structure of the deal.

## Withdrawal Deadlines: From Open-Ended Presence to Fixed Dates

The most politically important issue was the timetable for U.S. withdrawal.

For years, critics of the U.S. presence had feared that Washington intended to maintain permanent bases in Iraq. Iraqi factions demanded explicit language ruling out an indefinite occupation. The final agreement contained two major deadlines:

### 1. Withdrawal from Iraqi cities by June 30, 2009

U.S. combat forces were required to withdraw from Iraqi cities, towns, and villages by **June 30, 2009**. After that date, American troops were to operate from bases and conduct missions only in coordination with Iraqi authorities.

This deadline was highly symbolic. It allowed Maliki’s government to claim that Iraqi forces were taking the lead in securing urban areas. June 30 later became known in Iraq as “National Sovereignty Day.”

### 2. Complete withdrawal by December 31, 2011

The agreement required all U.S. forces to withdraw from Iraqi territory by **December 31, 2011**.

This was one of the most significant concessions in the pact. It transformed the U.S. military presence from an open-ended deployment into a temporary one with a fixed legal endpoint. The agreement stated that the presence of American forces was at the request of the Iraqi government and was not permanent.

The 2011 deadline later became central to U.S. and Iraqi politics. President Barack Obama, who took office in January 2009, implemented the withdrawal schedule, and the last U.S. troops left Iraq in December 2011, although U.S. forces later returned in a different capacity after the rise of the Islamic State.

## Jurisdiction Over American Troops

Another major dispute involved legal jurisdiction over U.S. military personnel.

From 2003 onward, American troops and many contractors had broad immunity from Iraqi prosecution. Iraqi leaders and much of the public viewed this as a violation of sovereignty, especially after incidents involving civilian casualties and contractor misconduct. The 2007 Blackwater shooting in Baghdad’s Nisour Square intensified Iraqi demands for accountability.

The final agreement created a divided jurisdictional arrangement.

### U.S. jurisdiction

The United States retained primary jurisdiction over American troops for actions committed:

- while on duty;
- on U.S. bases or agreed facilities;
- during authorized military operations.

This was important to Washington because it protected soldiers from being routinely subject to Iraqi criminal courts while carrying out military missions.

### Iraqi jurisdiction

Iraq gained jurisdiction over U.S. service members and civilian Defense Department personnel in a narrower category of cases: **grave premeditated felonies committed outside duty and outside agreed facilities**.

In practical terms, this meant Iraq could prosecute American personnel only under limited circumstances. The agreement required procedures to determine whether an alleged offense occurred on duty or off duty, and disputes could be handled through joint U.S.–Iraqi mechanisms.

Even though the Iraqi jurisdiction provision was limited, it was politically significant. It marked a major departure from the sweeping immunity that foreign forces had previously enjoyed under the occupation-era legal framework.

## Operations and Iraqi Sovereignty

The pact also addressed military operations more broadly. U.S. forces could no longer conduct unilateral operations as freely as before. Operations were to be carried out with the agreement of the Iraqi government and coordinated with Iraqi authorities.

The agreement also included language stating that the United States would not use Iraqi land, sea, or airspace as a launching point for attacks against other countries. This was especially important to Iraqi leaders concerned about relations with Iran and Syria. Iraq did not want to be seen as a platform for U.S. regional military action.

These provisions helped Maliki argue that the pact restored Iraqi sovereignty while still allowing cooperation with U.S. forces during the transition.

## Iraqi Political Debate and Approval

The agreement faced strong criticism inside Iraq. Supporters of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr denounced it as a continuation of occupation. Some Sunni and nationalist figures worried about either excessive U.S. influence or abandonment, depending on their political perspective. Kurdish parties were generally more supportive of a continued American role, seeing U.S. forces as a stabilizing presence.

Maliki’s government worked to secure enough parliamentary support by emphasizing the fixed withdrawal dates and the gains in Iraqi jurisdiction. The cabinet approved the agreement in November 2008, and the Iraqi parliament ratified it on **November 27, 2008**.

The agreement entered into force on **January 1, 2009**, replacing the U.N. mandate.

## Significance of the Negotiations

The 2008 security pact negotiations marked a turning point in U.S.–Iraq relations. They shifted the relationship from one based on occupation and international mandate to one formally based on Iraqi consent and bilateral agreement.

For Maliki, the negotiations were a test of political survival and nationalist credibility. By obtaining authorization to seek amendments, he demonstrated that Iraqi leaders were not passively accepting American demands. The final text gave him concrete achievements to present: a withdrawal from cities, a full withdrawal deadline, limits on U.S. operations, and some Iraqi jurisdiction over American personnel.

For the United States, the agreement preserved the legal framework needed to continue military operations temporarily, but it also required acceptance of a defined end date. Washington’s reluctance to renegotiate reflected concern that too many concessions could restrict U.S. forces or expose them to legal risk, yet the final deal showed that Iraqi sovereignty concerns could not be ignored.

## Conclusion

The 2008 U.S.–Iraq security pact was shaped by a difficult compromise. Maliki, under domestic pressure, was authorized to present amendments demanding stronger assertions of Iraqi sovereignty. The United States resisted reopening the agreement but ultimately accepted language and provisions that made Iraqi approval possible. The final pact established two landmark deadlines: U.S. withdrawal from Iraqi cities by **June 30, 2009**, and full withdrawal by **December 31, 2011**. It also altered the legal status of American troops by granting Iraq limited jurisdiction over serious off-duty crimes committed outside U.S. facilities.

The negotiations revealed the changing balance between Washington and Baghdad. Five years after the invasion, Iraq’s government was still dependent on U.S. military support, but it was also increasingly able to impose political and legal conditions on that support. The agreement became the legal bridge between the occupation era and the formal end of the U.S. military mission in Iraq in 2011.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a wire-service report datelined Baghdad explaining Iraq’s proposed amendments to the status-of-forces agreement with Washington and summarizing the political opposition and legal issues involved.
counterfactuals.output:
BAGHDAD — Iraq is seeking changes to a proposed status-of-forces agreement with the United States that would govern the presence of American troops after the expiration of the U.N. mandate, Iraqi officials said, as political opposition and unresolved legal questions continued to delay approval of the pact.

The draft agreement, negotiated by Baghdad and Washington, is intended to replace the U.N. Security Council authorization for U.S.-led forces in Iraq and set the terms for their operations, legal status and eventual withdrawal. Iraqi officials have said the government wants clearer limits on U.S. military activity and stronger guarantees of Iraqi sovereignty before submitting the accord for final approval.

Among the amendments sought by Iraqi negotiators are provisions clarifying the timetable for the withdrawal of U.S. forces, restrictions on raids and detentions, and language defining when U.S. soldiers and contractors could be subject to Iraqi law. Iraqi leaders also want assurances that Iraqi territory will not be used as a base for attacks on neighboring countries.

The legal status of U.S. personnel remains one of the most sensitive issues. Washington has traditionally sought immunity for its troops from local prosecution while deployed abroad. Iraqi politicians, however, face strong public pressure to ensure accountability, particularly in cases involving civilian deaths or actions conducted outside agreed military operations.

The proposed pact has exposed deep divisions within Iraq’s governing coalition and among opposition blocs. Supporters argue that a negotiated agreement is necessary to avoid a legal vacuum once the U.N. mandate expires and to provide an orderly framework for security cooperation and troop withdrawal. They say Iraq’s armed forces still need U.S. support in logistics, intelligence, air power and training.

Opponents say the agreement could legitimize a continued foreign military presence and compromise Iraqi sovereignty. Some Shiite factions, including followers of anti-U.S. cleric Moqtada al-Sadr, have rejected any pact allowing American troops to remain. Sunni and Kurdish leaders have raised separate concerns, with some seeking guarantees that U.S. support will not end abruptly before Iraqi forces are ready.

The agreement also faces constitutional and procedural questions. Iraqi lawmakers have debated whether the pact can be approved by the cabinet alone or must be ratified by parliament. Many legislators insist that any accord affecting sovereignty, foreign troops and criminal jurisdiction requires parliamentary approval. Some political figures have called for a national referendum.

The United States has pressed for completion of the deal before the U.N. mandate expires, warning that without a legal framework its forces would lack authority to operate in Iraq. Iraqi officials say they will not accept any agreement that does not reflect the country’s sovereignty and the government’s need to answer to parliament and the public.

Negotiations are continuing, but officials on both sides have acknowledged that time is short. Failure to reach an agreement could force Washington and Baghdad to seek an extension of the U.N. mandate or adopt temporary arrangements to prevent disruption of military operations.
